highlights.quote: a great American in whose symbolic shadow we stand today
highlights.note: King borrows Lincoln's authority to legitimize the march itself, a classic ethos-by-association move before he has made any substantive claim.

highlights.quote: In a sense, we've come to our nation's capital to cash a check.
highlights.note: The promissory-note conceit is the closest thing to a structured argument (promise made, promise broken, debt now owed) in the whole speech, though it is a moral analogy rather than verifiable market evidence.

highlights.quote: A check which has come back marked insufficient funds.
highlights.note: A visceral, concrete image of betrayal that converts abstract injustice into a feeling of being personally cheated.

highlights.quote: This is no time to engage in the luxury of cooling off
highlights.note: Presses the audience to feel the moment's urgency rather than wait, with no data or timeline attached, just moral pressure.

highlights.quote: will have a rude awakening if the nation returns to business As Usual.
highlights.note: A warning pitched entirely at emotional and moral stakes, not at any measurable consequence.

highlights.quote: We must not allow our creative protests to degenerate into physical violence.
highlights.note: King stakes the movement's credibility on nonviolent discipline, a direct trust-building claim aimed at skeptical onlookers.

highlights.quote: We hold these truths to be self-evident that all men Are Created Equal.
highlights.note: Grounds his claim in the borrowed authority of the Declaration of Independence rather than in any new evidence, asking the nation to be true to its own founding credibility.

highlights.quote: To Join Hands With Little White Boys And White Girls As Sisters And Brothers.
highlights.note: The speech's most iconic image of reconciliation, pure emotional aspiration with no mechanism for how it would come about.

highlights.quote: and we are calling it iPhone.
highlights.note: The naming reveal collapses three separate product categories (widescreen iPod, phone, internet communicator) into one falsifiable product claim, rather than an emotional appeal.

highlights.quote: multi-touch, which is phenomenal. It works like magic.
highlights.note: A mechanism claim for the enabling technology behind the touch interface, immediately followed by a live demo that lets the audience verify it themselves.

highlights.quote: really serious about software should make their own hardware.
highlights.note: Borrows the authority of industry pioneer Alan Kay to justify Apple's integrated hardware-and-software strategy — credibility by association.

highlights.quote: something wonderful for your hand. Just wonderful.
highlights.note: A pure sensory/aesthetic appeal to physical delight in the object, with no functional or evidentiary content.
A third party's spontaneous emotional reaction, quoted back to the audience as social proof of delight rather than as a technical claim.

highlights.quote: how thrilled I am to make the first public phone call with iPhone.
highlights.note: Genuine, unscripted human emotion during a live, high-stakes demo — the risk of the moment itself generates the pathos.
Textbook market-math logos: a quantifiable, independently checkable claim about market opportunity, exactly the kind of arithmetic a skeptical listener could verify.

highlights.quote: I skate to where the puck is going to be, not where it has been.
highlights.note: A closing borrowed-authority quote (Wayne Gretzky) that recasts Apple's history as visionary foresight, sealing the credibility argument on the way out.

airbnb_seed_deck_2008.title: Airbnb (then AirBed & Breakfast) — original seed pitch deck, 2008
airbnb_seed_deck_2008.medium: static slide deck — NOT a recorded/spoken pitch
airbnb_seed_deck_2008.note_on_medium: No recording of the actual investor-room delivery exists. Unlike every other entry in this project, there is no transcript or timing data here — this is a structural/textual analysis of the slides themselves, included because the deck's hook strategy (validate market size before the concept can be doubted) is a genuinely different rhetorical move than the Pathos-first opening the video corpus shows, and worth holding up as a contrast case.

verified_facts.raised: $600,000 from Sequoia Capital and Y Ventures
verified_facts.context: Used to pitch angel investors after launching at SXSW 2007 and the 2008 Democratic National Convention, before entering Y Combinator's Winter 2009 batch
verified_facts.cover_tagline: Book rooms with locals, rather than hotels.
verified_facts.slide_count_note: Sources disagree on exact count (10, 11, or 14 depending on how title/appendix slides are counted) — this analysis follows the commonly-cited ~11-slide structure: cover, problem, solution, market validation, market size, product, business model, adoption strategy, competition, competitive advantages, team.

slides.note: "Book rooms with locals, rather than hotels" — a one-line reframe, not a market claim yet. Pathos in the loosest sense: it's designed to be memorable and slightly provocative, priming curiosity rather than pain (unlike the video corpus's opening problem-hook).
Framed as a booking/pricing inefficiency, not a human story — logical framing from the first substantive slide.
Mechanism-first: how the marketplace connects supply and demand.

This is the deck's real hook, per the user's own read: proof people already want it (SXSW and DNC traction) placed early, before investors can dismiss the concept as too weird — the opposite sequencing from a Pathos-led opening.
TAM-style sizing — pure Logos, no emotional framing.
Product screenshots / booking flow.
Take-rate / revenue mechanics.
Go-to-market plan, still numbers-first.
Positioning against Craigslist/Couchsurfing/hotels.
First appearance of an Ethos-flavored claim — why this team's approach is defensible.
Closes on founder credibility, same rubric slot and same appeal as the Team phase in the video corpus — this is the one place the two pitch styles converge.

airbnb_seed_deck_2008.summary: Where the scored video corpus opens on Pathos and saves Logos for the middle, Airbnb's deck is Logos-led almost start to finish — it substitutes 'proof people already want this' for an emotional hook, because a two-sided marketplace pitched to seed investors has to defeat skepticism about the concept itself before anything else can land. Ethos is compressed into the final two slides, same position as the video corpus's Team phase, suggesting that closing-on-credibility may hold across pitch formats even when everything before it differs.

uber_pitch_deck_2008.title: UberCab — original pre-seed pitch deck, 2008
uber_pitch_deck_2008.medium: static slide deck — NOT a recorded/spoken pitch
uber_pitch_deck_2008.note_on_medium: Like the Airbnb deck, no recording of the actual investor-room delivery exists. The original ran roughly 25 slides; grouped here into 16 sections for readability, following the full slide-by-slide order confirmed via TechCrunch's 2023 teardown (see sources).

verified_facts.context: Pitched while the company was still called UberCab, before the app existed — a digital-hailing black-car service, years before rideshare drivers or the Uber name.
verified_facts.slide_count_note: The original deck ran ~25 slides; grouped here into 16 sections. Full slide-by-slide order verified via TechCrunch's 2023 teardown.

slides.note: Title page under the UberCab name — no tagline-driven hook, just the company presenting itself.
Frames aging fleets and unreliable street-hailing as a daily frustration for urban professionals — the deck's one clearly Pathos-led moment.
Mechanism-first: replace street hailing with app-based digital hailing.

slides.slide: Product Walkthrough (1-Click, Differentiators, Operating Principles, Apps, Website)
slides.note: Five consecutive slides making one sustained Logos argument: the product is thought through end to end.
Restaurants, bars, shows, airports — concrete scenarios that double as indirect demand validation.
Convenience-focused, but still argued benefit-by-benefit rather than through a single emotional story.
The deck's only nod toward 'evidence of impact' — an asserted sustainability benefit, not a measured one.
Mercedes S-class fleet spec and initial launch geography.
Predictive dispatch positioned as a durable technical moat.
The $4.2B U.S. taxi-and-limousine market, sized and segmented — pure Logos.
Expansion sequencing across priority metros.
A named best-case ($1B/yr revenue) against a realistic case ($20-30M/yr profit) — an aggressive claim still argued in numbers.
BlackBerry 32% / Windows Mobile 30% / iPhone 10% — a timing argument built entirely on adoption data.
Roadmap and go-to-market ideas, still numbers- and plan-first.
A $3.5B-by-2010 delivery-market aside, extending the sizing argument beyond rides.
Reserved domain, filed provisional patent, bank/PayPal accounts, 15 signed clients, 3 purchased vehicles — proof of execution, not a story. Notably: this deck has no dedicated team-bio slide at all.

uber_pitch_deck_2008.summary: UberCab's earliest deck is almost entirely Logos, start to finish, with two brief Pathos beats (the problem framing and the environmental-benefits aside) and no Ethos until the very last slide's traction proof. Unlike Airbnb, it has no team slide whatsoever — the pitch bets everything on the strength of the market-sizing and 'why now' argument, not on founder credibility. Evidence of Impact barely registers here either, appearing only as an aside — a pattern this project also found in the general VC-deck corpus, not just Airbnb.

dropbox_seed_deck_2007.title: Dropbox — original seed pitch deck, 2007
dropbox_seed_deck_2007.medium: static slide deck — NOT a recorded/spoken pitch
dropbox_seed_deck_2007.note_on_medium: No recording of the Y Combinator demo-day delivery exists. Sources disagree on exact slide count (commonly cited as 17; a separately-circulated redesigned template runs to 24) — this analysis follows the 9 core beats corroborated across multiple independent teardowns (see sources).

verified_facts.raised: $1.2 million seed round led by Sequoia Capital
verified_facts.context: Presented at Y Combinator Summer 2007 demo day; the deck was later shared publicly by Sequoia Capital itself.
verified_facts.slide_count_note: Commonly cited as 17 slides; grouped here into 9 core beats corroborated across independent teardowns rather than a full slide-by-slide reconstruction.

slides.note: Brand-first title slide.
A structured agenda up front — a small, procedural credibility signal (this founder has a plan).
Four words, one image, then four concrete reasons (multiple computers, team sharing, photos/videos online, USB drives as a stopgap). About as Pathos-led as a technical product slide gets.
One of the most quoted lines in pitch-deck history — but the slide itself argues reliability and mechanism, not feeling.
Walks the actual product experience rather than describing it abstractly.

slides.slide: Competitive Analysis ("Why Our Competitors Screw Up")
slides.note: Named competitors, checkmarks and X's — a direct, evidence-style comparison.
Three revenue segments (individual freemium, SMB licensing, desktop-to-web) laid out as mechanics, not vision.
Free-account acquisition and viral growth strategy, still numbers-first.
Closes on peer-ranked social proof rather than a founder-bio slide — credibility borrowed from a cohort standing, not from personal history. Like Uber's deck, there is no dedicated team slide.

dropbox_seed_deck_2007.summary: Dropbox's deck opens on the sharpest Pathos hook of any deck in this set ('Storage is a mess') and then, like every other deck here, spends the rest of its runtime almost entirely in Logos — competitive comparison, business model, go-to-market. It closes on Ethos through borrowed social proof (a YC cohort ranking) rather than a team-credentials slide, meaning two of these four historical decks (Dropbox and Uber) skip a dedicated Team slide entirely. Evidence of Impact never appears — unsurprising for a productivity tool with no social-outcome claim to make.

linkedin_series_b_deck_2004.title: LinkedIn — Series B pitch deck to Greylock, 2004
linkedin_series_b_deck_2004.medium: static slide deck — NOT a recorded/spoken pitch
linkedin_series_b_deck_2004.note_on_medium: Reid Hoffman published this deck himself in 2013 along with his own slide-by-slide retrospective commentary — the richest primary source of any deck in this set. The original ran 38 slides plus a 5-slide appendix, unusually long and narrative-heavy by modern standards; grouped here into 17 sections for readability.

verified_facts.context: LinkedIn was about a year old and pre-revenue, with under 1 million users versus Friendster's 10.5 million and MySpace's 2.5 million at the time — this is a Series B, not a seed pitch, and it shows: it argues from a full year of Series A execution, not just a concept.
verified_facts.cover_tagline: Find and contact the people you need through the people you already trust.
verified_facts.slide_count_note: 38 slides plus a 5-slide appendix, grouped here into 17 sections. Reid Hoffman's own slide-by-slide commentary is public at reidhoffman.org.

slides.note: Opens with three explicit questions investors must answer yes to — argument structure first, no hook.
Three product lines previewed early, with an honest acknowledgment of uncertainty about which would lead.
Names three business problems and explains structurally why existing solutions fail (adverse selection, weak reputation systems) — logic, not a personal story.
The foundational thesis: networks, not directories, solve the problem.

slides.slide: Proof by Analogy: eBay, PayPal, Google
slides.note: Three consecutive slides arguing the same thesis by borrowed precedent. Hoffman's own retrospective calls this stretch 'one of the strongest parts of the presentation' — Logos through analogy, not through LinkedIn's own data.
Positions against Monster and LexisNexis using the same network-effect logic just established.

slides.slide: Series A vs. Series B Performance
slides.note: Honestly shows LinkedIn trailing both Friendster and MySpace on raw user count, then argues why trajectory still supports leadership — Logos even when the number itself isn't flattering.
Splits competitors into social (Friendster, MySpace, Orkut) versus professional (Ryze, OpenBC, Spoke, ZeroDegrees).
Organizational endorsements — which Hoffman himself later called 'mostly a mistake slide,' a rare founder's own verdict on an Ethos move that didn't land.
Hoffman hedges here: he later admits neither showcased partnership 'delivered substantive value.'
Asserts viral dynamics without over-explaining — Hoffman calls virality 'a pretty deep secret in the industry at the time.'
Three slides reinforcing 'build the network first, monetize on top,' using eBay/PayPal/Google as monetization precedent.
Hoffman's own advice in hindsight: don't linger on TAM slides — they signal you don't understand the business bottom-up.

slides.slide: Product Roadmap: InLeads, Job Listings, Subscriptions
slides.note: Six slides of concrete product mockups and launch dates — 'show, don't tell,' per Hoffman, though he flags the customer-quote slide here as weak execution of that principle.
Hoffman notes the prior round's projections proved 'approximately accurate' — an unusually strong credibility claim delivered entirely through numbers.
Names each leader's specific domain expertise (ops scale, social-space experience, technical depth, product-market fit, generalist capability) rather than generic bios.
Closes on Sequoia's name, prior capital well spent, and a reprised opening thesis — which Hoffman later critiques as a missed chance to unify the deck's frame.

linkedin_series_b_deck_2004.summary: The most purely Logos-driven deck in this set — Pathos never clearly surfaces once across all 38 slides. It argues almost entirely by borrowed analogy (eBay, PayPal, Google), honest trend-lines, and mechanism, saving Ethos for exactly two moments: the Team slide and the closing Investors/ask slide, both near the end — the same structural position as the 'Team' close in every other deck studied here, including the real judged pitches. Being a Series B rather than a seed pitch, it also argues from a year of Series A execution instead of pure concept, which is likely why it can afford to be almost entirely evidence-driven.
